_README: Every actorId and every field name below is UNVERIFIED. apify.com was unreachable
from the environment this was built in, so nothing here was checked against a live
actor. Run `npm run probe-actor -- <source>` with APIFY_TOKEN set: it runs the actor
once, saves the raw dataset to .probe/, and prints the real field inventory.
Then correct `input.fields` and `map` here. No code change is needed for a remap.
input.fields maps our canonical knob -> the actor's own input key. null means the
actor does not support that knob; the pipeline filters client-side where it can.
map values are ordered candidate paths (dot notation, [n] for array index). The first
path that yields a non-empty value wins, so listing several variants keeps a run alive
through minor actor changes. A miss on a `required` field aborts that source loudly.

upwork.verified_at: 2026-09-09, schema read from build 1.0.24. searchQueries confirmed as the search field.

unmapped_knobs.note: Declared but not wired. budget is the interesting one: filtering low budgets at the source would stop us paying for $5 postings at all. Its enum values are not printed by the probe, so wiring it is a separate change with its own verification.

upwork.schema_notes: Declared inputs: searchQueries (array), maxItems, sort (relevance+desc | recency+desc | spend+desc), jobType, experienceLevel, workload, duration, budget, clientHires, proxyConfiguration. There is no recency input, hence sort=recency+desc plus a client-side window. Two guesses failed before this: searchQuery and queries were both accepted and silently ignored.
upwork.mapping_notes: Upwork returns no company name and no location: both were NO HIT across every probe, and that is a property of the source, not a mapping gap. Postings are client-anonymous until you apply.
upwork.pricing_note: Measured, not assumed: two probe runs each billed $0.00005 for twenty results, which is $0.0025 per thousand. Effectively free, so the pre-check reserves almost nothing and every query runs. If the actor ever starts charging properly the global cap still catches it after one query.

linkedin.pricing_note: Measured, not assumed: 150 results billed $0.0557, which is $0.371 per thousand. The previous $6.00 figure was inherited from the retired smorgi_apps actor and was sixteen times too high. At the real rate a 150-result query costs about six cents and a full eighteen-query pass is about $1.00.

rejected.bebity/linkedin-jobs-scraper: $29.99/month rental, fixed fee outside the budget cap
rejected.smorgi_apps/linkedin-jobs-scraper: Permanently offline. Actor throws on start: "residential + Playwright unit economics; historical success below the keep gate. Not scheduled to return."

input.minItems_note: An earlier 400 suggested the actor enforces this floor. Not re-tested, and not worth re-testing: 150 fresh results cost about six cents, which is better coverage per dollar than a smaller page.

linkedin.schema_notes: Rich schema. keyword is an array and is NOT sufficient on its own: the actor refuses to build a search URL from keywords alone and exits with zero results, billing nothing. It needs at least one location, hence locations: ["United States"] in the template. Also useful and safe: publishedAt (r86400/r604800/r2592000), jobTitleExclude, excludeRecruitingAgencies, companySizeMin/Max, workType. workType would filter to remote at source but its accepted values are not printed by the probe, so remote stays a client-side judgement rather than a third guess. salaryBase offers an enum topping out at exactly the 120000 salary floor and is deliberately NOT wired: LinkedIn salary filters act on stated salary, so it would drop every posting that omits pay, which is most of the good ones, and never rejecting on missing compensation is a rule this pipeline is built around.
linkedin.cadence_note: Every other day, by request. The cost argument for it is gone now that the real rate is known: daily would be about $1.00 a run, well inside the cap. What it still buys is less duplicate churn, since LinkedIn has no result-level dedupe across runs and salaried postings turn over slowly. Set runEveryNDays to 1 for daily.
linkedin.verified_at: 2026-09-09, live run oxNoH1jA2Iydh2uYl. 150 items, all mapped fields resolved, $0.0557 billed.
linkedin.mapping_notes: From live runs: url/title/company/description/posted_at resolve 100%, comp_type_raw 100% via contractType, pay on about 61% of postings, poster_name on about 7%. salaryInfo is an array of amounts, ["$116000","$159500"] on the sample, so it maps to comp_min and comp_max by index. Reading only element 0 would have taken the BOTTOM of the range as the whole figure and rejected a $116k-$159.5k posting against the $120k floor. The array carries no period, so a posting quoting a rate rather than a salary arrives as a bare number labelled Full-time; score.js treats an implausibly small annual figure as unknown rather than rejecting on it. There is no expired flag. workType is deliberately NOT mapped to remote: it carries the job function, "Management and Manufacturing" on the sample, not the workplace type its input-schema label implies, and it resolved on every item.

indeed.schema_notes: Declared inputs: position, maxItemsPerSearch, country, location, parseCompanyDetails, saveOnlyUniqueItems, followApplyRedirects, startUrls. We had been sending maxItems and maxDaysOld, neither of which is declared. There is no recency input at all, so freshness is client-side only and daily runs will re-fetch the same top results. That is the duplicate billing the spend report tracks.
